consensus_summary: Across the blind responses, the primary meaning of justify/justification is the historic Protestant forensic sense: God’s legal declaration that a sinner is righteous and in right standing with Him through faith in Christ, typically by imputation of Christ’s righteousness rather than works; Catholic transformative, New Perspective covenantal, Orthodox participatory, and James’s demonstrative senses are listed as common or minority alternatives, with no full cross-tradition consensus on mechanism.
book_summary: The book defines justify as to judge, declare, or demonstrate a person, word, deed, or cause right against a charge (opposite: condemn), and states that God justifies the sinner through forgiveness in Christ, not by declaring wrongdoing right; it flags the once-for-all imputation-of-Christ’s-righteousness view as the common teaching it is distinguishing from.
consensus_core_identification: God’s forensic declaration that the sinner is righteous / has right standing, received by faith (classically via imputed righteousness).
book_core_identification: To judge, declare, or demonstrate someone or something right against a charge; applied to sinners, God does this through forgiveness in Christ, not by declaring wrongdoing right.
boundary_disagreement: The book elevates the broad lexical/judicial range (including demonstrating a word, deed, or cause right, and OT condemn-the-wicked / justify-the-righteous usage) into the primary definition and treats James-style demonstration as inside the core, while reclassifying the soteriological case as forgiveness-based and explicitly excluding the common imputation formula of declaring the believer righteous with Christ’s righteousness; consensus keeps that forensic-imputation reading as primary and treats demonstrative/OT/general senses as secondary alternatives.
material_contradiction: Apparent tension on the ungodly: consensus primary reading (e.g. Rom 4:5–6) holds that God justifies the ungodly by reckoning/imputing righteousness; the book, citing Prov 17:15 and its common-view note, insists God does not justify by declaring wrongdoing right and instead justifies through forgiveness. Whether this fully contradicts depends on equating ‘imputed righteousness’ with ‘declaring wrongdoing right,’ which classical Protestant accounts deny.
rationale: Minimum cores share the same general forensic category (declare/judge right vs. condemn) and the application that God justifies sinners in Christ, so this is not a replacement of referent (not DIVERGENT) nor an unmatched invention (not NOVEL). Differences are material at the boundary and mechanism: the book broadens the head definition beyond the consensus’s soteriology-first focus, folds ‘demonstrate’ and non-personal objects into the core, and deliberately parts from the commonly taught imputation account in favor of forgiveness without ‘declaring wrongdoing right.’ That is refinement of extension, conditions, and precision around a preserved category, not mere wording and not total core replacement.
strongest_objection: Romans 4:5–8 (printed with the entry) is the consensus’s central proof that God ‘justifieth the ungodly’ and ‘imputeth righteousness without works,’ so the book’s contrast with imputation and its appeal to Prov 17:15 may under-read Paul or mischaracterize the common view it rejects.
